corrections.license: None stated: no LICENSE file, and README.md and ug.pdf give no terms; prebuilt x86-64 Windows/Linux binaries only, used on top of the separately distributed CKTSO library
corrections.caveats: First-party results.pdf (CKTSO-GPU version 20221207; the PDF is dated 2022-12-07) only; no benchmark code is public and the solver source is not available (prebuilt x86-64 Windows/Linux libraries plus C/C++ demos), so this cannot be rerun. The GPU is compared only with CKTSO on ONE thread and with sequential KLU, not with multithreaded CKTSO, NICSLU, cuSOLVER or GLU, so the speedup is partly a GPU-vs-one-core comparison. The user guide (ug.pdf, version 20230325) itself says CKTSO-GPU cannot efficiently accelerate highly sparse circuit matrices, that plain CKTSO on multicore CPUs gives the best performance on extremely sparse ones, and recommends the GPU module only when flops/NNZ(L+U) > 50, where it 'tends to perform faster than CKTSO (1 thread)'; the 29 test matrices were selected with exactly that filter. KLU is given CKTSO's ordering. Compiler versions are stated (gcc 4.8.5, nvcc 11.0) but optimization flags are not. GpuRefactorize and GpuSolve take the matrix values and vectors in host memory, but results.pdf does not say whether the reported times include host-device transfers. disabledL1cache/readme.txt says some GPUs (V100 named) give wrong results unless L1 cache is disabled, at about 20% performance loss. No license text in the repo (reference only), and it needs the separately distributed CKTSO library. Last commit 2023-04-01 (GitHub commits page), more than 3 years before today, so abandoned. Per-matrix times appear only as bar charts.

notes: All numbers, versions, hardware and compilers in the record match results.pdf exactly; I only filled in the license text and added the user guide's own limits (GPU module worthwhile only for Flops/NNZ(L+U) > 50; multicore CPU CKTSO is best for very sparse matrices). This is a GPU add-on module of CKTSO (already listed), with its own repo, binaries and claims, so I kept it as a separate entry; fold it into the CKTSO entry if you prefer.

corrections.license: Proprietary prebuilt binaries with no source: use is gated by a license key file (nicslu202110/license/nicslu.lic), and license/readme.txt says 'License for research/trial purpose only. Long-term license key file is now provided.' The README says the license has been extended to 9999-99-99.
corrections.caveats: First-party 2019 results.pdf (NICSLU 201905B; the PDF is dated 2019-06-11). The newer nicslu202110 libraries were published afterwards and were not benchmarked there. No benchmark code and no source, so it cannot be rerun; 136 of the 182 matrices are 'real circuit cases' that the PDF does not identify as public. Compiler, flags and thread counts for every solver are unstated, and 'best configurations' is not defined. KLU is a sequential solver, so the 1.87X is likely multithreaded NICSLU against one-thread KLU. The README says NICSLU 'will no longer be updated or maintained' and points users to its successor CKTSO (already on the known list), which 'provides better performance and scalability'. The binaries need a research/trial license key file (nicslu202110/license), so this is reference only. Peer-reviewed support exists but was not opened: IEEE TCAD 2013 vol. 32 no. 2 pp. 261-274 ('NICSLU: An Adaptive Sparse Matrix Solver for Parallel Circuit Simulation'), whose abstract, seen only as a search-engine snippet (dl.acm.org, ieeexplore, researchgate and the Tsinghua lab site are egress-blocked), reports 2.08x to 8.57x geometric-mean speedups over KLU with 1-12 threads on the matrices (of 35) suited to the parallel algorithm. Linux libraries ship as lib_centos6_x64_gcc482_fma and _no_fma (gcc 4.8.2). Last commit 2026-03-22 ('Final update'), from the GitHub commits page.

notes: Every number in the record matches results.pdf. I filled in the license, which is a proprietary research/trial key-file license, so reference is right. The TCAD 2013 abstract (2.08x-8.57x geomean vs KLU, 1-12 threads, seen only as a search snippet) makes this a retier candidate to B for a session that can open IEEE/ACM.

corrections.baseline: Not verified from an opened page. Per search snippets only: the ACM TOMS 2016 GPU paper compares against 'a state-of-the-art multifrontal solver on a multicore CPU' (not named in the snippet); the Duff-Hogg-Lopez a-posteriori-threshold-pivoting paper (RAL-TR-2016-017 / NLAFET Working Note 21) compares SSIDS v2 with HSL_MA86, HSL_MA97 and PARDISO on a multicore machine. MUMPS is not named in either snippet.
corrections.claimed_speedup: No numbers in the repo. From search-engine snippets of paper abstracts (not opened): the TOMS 2016 paper says that for large indefinite problems SSIDS on a GPU achieves up to 4.6x over a state-of-the-art multifrontal solver on a multicore CPU; the APTP paper says SSIDS v2 'performs favorably' against HSL_MA86, HSL_MA97 and PARDISO on a multicore machine (no ratio in the snippet). An independent study (Swirydowicz et al., 'Linear solvers for power grid optimization problems: a review of GPU-accelerated linear solvers', Parallel Computing, arXiv 2106.13909) found, per snippet, that turning on GPU acceleration in SSIDS slowed it down compared with CPU-only, and that all GPU solvers tested were slower than one-thread MA57 on power-grid KKT matrices; on CPU, SSIDS was fastest for the smallest case (ACTIVSg2000).
corrections.caveats: Evidence not reachable: the SSIDS GPU paper (Hogg, Ovtchinnikov and Scott, ACM TOMS 42(1), 2016, doi 10.1145/2756548 as cited in the README; preprint RAL-P-2014-006 on epubs.stfc.ac.uk) and the CPU a-posteriori-pivoting report cited in docs/Fortran/ssids.rst are on egress-blocked hosts (doi.org, dl.acm.org, epubs.stfc.ac.uk, nlafet.eu, centaur.reading.ac.uk, osti.gov), so the figures in claimed_speedup come from search snippets only and no ratio is verified. A session that can open the TOMS paper or the APTP report could retier to B (peer reviewed, against HSL codes and PARDISO). Independent counter-evidence (Swirydowicz et al., Parallel Computing, per snippet): on power-grid optimization KKT matrices SSIDS's GPU mode was slower than its CPU mode and slower than one-thread MA57, so the GPU claim is workload dependent. The baselines are not in the catalog's list for this category (SuiteSparse, Eigen sparse, PETSc), so baseline_in_list is false. The library is Fortran with a C interface (callable from C++). The ChangeLog entry of 2016-09-23 says SSIDS v2 added CPU, multi-GPU and heterogeneous execution. SSIDS needs OMP_CANCELLATION=TRUE and OMP_PROC_BIND=TRUE or it fails with error -53 (README).
